Summary: ICO: consent-or-soft-opt-in rule applies to individual subscribers; "these rules only apply to individual subscribers (which includes sole traders and some types of partnership)". Law-firm guidance: can send promotional emails without consent to limited companies, LLPs, corporate bodies, but recipients need right to unsubscribe; identify business; keep suppression records. Corporate subscribers include companies, LLPs, Scottish partnerships, some govt bodies. GDPR lawful basis less settled: older SCL commentary says ICO staff said B2B marketing to identifiable business address allowed under PECR and GDPR without consent; same commentary argued a lawful basis (legitimate interests) still needed under UK GDPR. Sources mostly law-firm blogs.

QUERY: CASL Canada B2B cold email implied consent conspicuous publication exemption CRTC guidance business electronic address | MODE: standard | DOMAINS: none | DATE: 2026-10-20
Links: crtc.gc.ca/eng/com500/guide.htm ; mltaikins.com/casl/... ; cyberimpact.com/fr/blog/casl-compliance-must-know ; canadianelectricalwholesaler.ca/5-types-of-consent-part-4-implied-conspicuously-published/ ; blg.com publication_5139.pdf ; 14west.atlassian.net
Summary: CRTC guidance: publicly posted address can support implied consent only if "this conspicuous publication of their email address must not be accompanied by a statement indicating they do not want to receive CEMs at that address. If the statement is not present, in order to send a CEM, the message must relate to the recipient's business role, functions or duties in an official or business capacity." Secondary sources: two-year window (unclear start); "B2B does not mean exempt" practitioner summary: finding a business email and pitching does not create the relationship; for most B2B cold emailing need valid express or implied consent. Burden of proof on sender. Compu.Finder (CRTC 2017-368): non-functional unsubscribe found noncompliant ("the unsubscribe mechanism did not satisfy the requirements of CASL"). Only CRTC page primary.

QUERY: Australia Spam Act 2003 B2B cold email inferred consent conspicuous publication ACMA business email address unsubscribe | MODE: standard | DOMAINS: none | DATE: 2026-10-20
Links: itomic.com.au/?p=3056 ; pointonpartners.com.au/spam-act/ ; mondaq.com/australia/consumer-law/996226/spamming-and-the-spam-act ; legislation.gov.au Spam Act 2003 ; emaillistvalidation.com/blog/conspicuously-published-address-rule-australian-spam-act/ ; organicwebs.com.au
Summary: ACMA guidance (quoted by Itomic): consent can be inferred from conspicuous publication only if address publicly accessible, carries no statement that commercial messages are unwanted, and message relates directly to recipient's role. Itomic: strong link needed between promotion and recipient's role; cannot infer consent because you believe product would benefit them; example: IT department address allows IT pitch to that department. Pointon Partners and Mondaq: consent may not be inferred from mere fact that relevant address was published. Commercial message must contain functional unsubscribe facility. One vendor blog says address must be prominent, footer link not enough; ACMA-quoted text defines conspicuous only as publicly accessible (blog's reading is its own).
